result:
The rain isn't falling so much as it is arriving. That's the difference nobody ever points out in those poems. Falling suggests a purpose, a trajectory toward something specific. Arriving suggests the window has been waiting, or that the sky has been holding something until it decided this particular pane of glass, on a Tuesday, was the moment.

I keep a mug of tea going cold at my elbow, watching the droplets merge into rivulets that argue with each other over the glass. Two streams meet, one swallows the other, and the loser disappears into the larger current. I find this more honest than most of the politics on the television behind me. The smaller stream doesn't argue. It just gets absorbed.

There's a cat on the fire escape three stories down. It watches the rain the way I do. Not with urgency. With the particular boredom of a creature that has decided, after considerable philosophical reflection, that the weather is a fact and not a problem. I want to be that cat. I want to look up from the glass and find that I've been sitting here for an hour, that my tea has forgotten its original purpose, that I have achieved the exact, quiet, useless state I've been trying to engineer for years.

The rivulet reaches the bottom and hangs there, trembling, refusing to fully commit to the window frame.

It will fall in a moment. It won't. Either way, it's the most interesting thing I've seen all day.
